title: Stephen Saad and Africa's First Generic ARV, Port Elizabeth, 2003
dek: Working through licences from patent holders, Aspen launched a locally made antiretroviral in August 2003 and built a plant to make more.

story.event: Launching Aspen-Stavudine, the first generic antiretroviral developed and made in Africa, under voluntary licences
story.summary: After taking a voluntary licence from GlaxoSmithKline in October 2001 on narrow terms (South African public sector only, no exports), Stephen Saad's Aspen Pharmacare launched Aspen-Stavudine in August 2003, the first generic antiretroviral developed and manufactured in Africa, made in Port Elizabeth and priced 17 to 41 per cent below the originator. After a Competition Commission finding against GSK and Boehringer Ingelheim in October 2003, licences widened; in January 2005 Aspen became the first generic maker cleared by the US FDA to supply ARVs under PEPFAR.
paragraphs: On 6 August 2003, Aspen Pharmacare announced Aspen-Stavudine, an antiretroviral developed by its own scientists and made at its plant in Port Elizabeth. Its chief executive, Stephen Saad, called it the first generic ARV developed and manufactured in Africa, "a solution to what is largely an African problem". Saad had started Aspen in 1997, aged 33, as a small sales business run from a suburban house; by 2003 it was southern Africa's largest maker of generic medicines.

The drug rested on a choice made two years earlier: to work through licences from patent holders rather than around them. In October 2001 GlaxoSmithKline gave Aspen a voluntary licence for AZT, 3TC and the combination Combivir; it already held one from Bristol-Myers Squibb for stavudine and didanosine. The GSK terms were narrow. Aspen could sell only to South Africa's public sector and could not export, and by one report at the time it was to pass 30 per cent of net profit to local NGOs. Saad said Aspen could now offer the government "more affordable anti-retrovirals for the South African population". The same report noted that success would depend on how the government responded.

Aspen spent the next two years developing and registering its own versions, and was adding a new tablet-making facility in Port Elizabeth at a time, the company said, when pharmaceutical manufacturing was being withdrawn from South Africa. Stavudine was priced 17 to 41 per cent below the originator brand. Saad called it one part of a wider response that also needed nutrition, education and prevention.

Not everyone wanted the voluntary route. Activists pressed for compulsory licences, and in October 2003 a complaint brought by patient groups including the Treatment Action Campaign led the Competition Commission to find that GSK and Boehringer Ingelheim had abused their dominant positions. GSK widened Aspen's licence to private buyers that month, and in December both companies settled by licensing more generic makers.

In January 2005 Aspen became the first generic maker cleared by the US Food and Drug Administration to supply ARVs under the American PEPFAR programme, and in the government's tender that March it won eight of fifteen drug categories.

quote.text: Since victory and defeat there must be, the victory to be philosophically prayed for is that of the more inclusive side,--of the side which even in the hour of triumph will to some degree do justice to the ideals in which the vanquished party's interests lay.
quote.work: The Will to Believe, and Other Essays in Popular Philosophy
quote.locator: "The Moral Philosopher and the Moral Life", section III
quote.source_title: The Will to Believe, and Other Essays in Popular Philosophy, Project Gutenberg eBook #26659
quote.connection: Aspen's licences were the kind of settlement James hoped for, leaving the patent holders something of what they valued. Yet the wider settlement of December 2003 came after activists refused to settle and took the companies to the Competition Commission, a part of the story his principle does not easily account for.

reflection: Saad chose to work with the patent holders, on tight terms, rather than wait for a fight to be won. Others did fight, and their fight widened what his licences allowed. It is hard to say how far his route would have gone without them.

When you deal with someone much larger than you, a hospital group, a funder, a supplier, you will be offered terms that feel too narrow. Sometimes they are the way in. It helps to know, before you agree, what you are giving up for now and what you still hope someone will push to change.
invitation: Pick one agreement you are working under or negotiating. Write a single line naming the term you accepted only to get started, and the date you will ask to revisit it.

research_notes: The 30 per cent: Down To Earth (November 2001) says Aspen pays no royalty and gives 30 per cent of net profit to South African NGOs, on a no-profit basis; other contemporary accounts found in search snippets (aidsmap, IRIN) describe 30 per cent of net sales, or a 30 per cent licensing fee from GSK and Shire set aside for NGOs, but those pages were blocked (403) and could not be read, so the story gives the Down To Earth version and attributes it to 'one report at the time'. Licence scope: Pharmafile says the 2001 licence covered the public sector only and was extended to the private sector in October 2003; a GSK statement quoted in search results also mentions sub-Saharan Africa, but no loadable source confirmed it, so the story says only 'private buyers'. FDA: Business Report (December 2004) reported FDA approval of the Port Elizabeth plant, the first for an African manufacturer, while the Mail & Guardian (January 2005) and Health-e date the approval of the generic ARVs themselves to January 2005; the story uses January 2005 for clearance to supply under PEPFAR. The Mail & Guardian calls Aspen the first drug manufacturer in the world to win FDA approval for generic ARVs; Health-e says the first generic manufacturer approved to supply PEPFAR; the story uses the narrower PEPFAR wording. The Aspen quotations are from the company's own press release and Down To Earth; no longer interview with Saad about the decision could be found or loaded (a 2025 BusinessTech profile and the Nelson Mandela University honorary doctorate citation were blocked or timed out), so the story describes the decision through documented terms and statements rather than his later reflections. Health-e (via Financial Mail) reports that the annual cost of first-line ARV treatment fell from over R95,000 to around R1,200 in five years, largely because of generics; it is a single-source figure and was left out of the story. The 'activists pressed for compulsory licences' line comes from Health-e (2005); the Competition Commission complaint is from Pharmafile. Founding: Brand South Africa credits Saad with founding Aspen in 1997 aged 33 in a suburban home; the story does not discuss co-founders. Port Elizabeth is now Gqeberha; the story uses the name of the time.
